lines: Somebody drops a field they're sure nobody's using anymore.
Nothing stops them. Nothing even warns them.
And for days, everyone still reading that field just quietly sees nothing where a value used to be.
An earlier fix assumed a record's fields still mean exactly what they meant when it was first written.
That assumption needs something actually enforcing it, not just hoping everyone plays along.
That enforcement is the whole reason this exists at all.
Worth reasoning through before the reveal settles it.
Same change, same dropped field, but checked against a stricter rule this time instead of a lenient one.
Does the stricter rule actually catch it, or does it slip through just the same?
answer: It catches it, and that's exactly the point of choosing a stricter rule.
Checked against what still-reading consumers actually depend on, this change simply never ships.
The rule that was active, not the change itself, decided whether anyone noticed in time.

lines: One direction asks whether something newer can still make sense of something older.
The other direction asks the exact opposite question instead.
And one stricter option refuses to take anyone's word for it, checking every version that's ever existed.
Drop a field, and the lenient direction shrugs it off without complaint.
Require a brand-new one with nothing to fall back on, and that same direction refuses outright.
Same kind of change on paper. Completely different outcome, depending only on which rule is actually watching.
Worth reasoning through once more before this reveal settles it.
The same rename, kept in its original spot, run past three different ways of describing a record's shape.
Does every one of them treat that rename the same way?
answer: One of them couldn't care less what anything is called, only where it sits.
Give that one the same spot under a different name, and it never even notices the difference.

lines: One of these three tracks identity by name, falling back on a stated default when a name goes missing.
Another tracks identity by position instead, so a rename passes clean but reusing that same position does not.
And the third was never really built with any of this in mind, so somebody else has to make the rules up for it.
How types get grouped together for checking is its own separate decision, worth making on purpose.
And out on the wire, nobody sends the whole description along with every single message.
Just a small tag pointing back to wherever the full description already lives.
Every figure in this reel came from one real run, happening just now, of this topic's own toy models.
The rule that caught what a looser one would have missed.
And the small tag that made the full round trip and still came back exactly right.
So: pick the rule that actually matches who's upgrading first.
Know that not every format agrees on what even counts as the same field.
And remember that passing every one of these checks still isn't the same as being right.
